To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cocaine-induced LPT in the ventral Tegmental area is mediated by D5 receptors and NMDA receptors, and that it requires protein synthesis and increases the synaptic content of GluR1 AMPA receptors, and it shares the same molecular substrats for its expression with STD-LTP.
cocaine induces LTP-like changes on VTA synapses that are not evident until 3 h after exposure and that are mediated via activation of dopamine D5 receptors and protein synthesis.

cocaine induces a long-term potentiation in the VTA that is expressed 3 h after drug exposure and is mediated via D5 receptor activation and requires protein synthesis, and that the same molecular mechanisms are shared between this cocaine-induced LTP and activity-dependent LTP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of action and the time course of cocaine-induced LTP, and its relationship with the STD-LTP induced in the same region.
the mechanism of cocaine-induced LTP and the relationship between this form of plasticity and the STD form.
the mechanism and time course of cocaine-induced LTP in the VTA and the possible role that this form of synaptic plasticity might play in the acquisition of drug addiction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cocaine exposure induces an LTP-like plasticity in the VTA that is not detectible minutes after drug exposure, but fully expressed within 1 h.
cocaine induces an LTP-like synaptic enhancement in the VTA that shares the same mechanisms of expression as activity-dependent LTP and that is expressed with a delay of several hours.
cocaine exposure induces a form of long-lasting synaptic plasticity in the VTA, and that the molecular mechanisms of cocaine-induced LTP and activity-dependent LTP are similar.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cocaine exposure induces a form of LTD in the VTA.
the cocaine-induced LTP in the VTA is an activity-dependent process that involves the same molecular mechanisms as STD-LTP and is expressed by a delayed increase in GluR1 expression.

cocaine exposure induces a long-lasting enhancement in AMPA-mediated transmission in the VTA, and this is mediated via D5 receptors and protein synthesis, and it is expressed via a GluR1-dependent mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the time course of cocaine-induced LTP is much longer than that of LTP induced by activity-dependent STD protocols, which is consistent with the idea that drug exposure is not a physiological trigger for LTP induction.
cocaine exposure induces LTP-like plasticity in the VTA that shares some of the molecular mechanisms with activity-dependent LPT.
cocaine exposure induces an LTP-like synaptic potentiation that is not detectible minutes after exposure but is fully evident within 3 h and that shares molecular substrates with STD-LTP.
